analysis.one_liner: Caps prison commissary prices at local retail levels and bans revenue-sharing vendor contracts.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in the House Judiciary Committee since its introduction, with no committee action, no floor vote, and no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the federal Bureau of Prisons to price every item in prison commissaries no higher than the ordinary retail price in the state where the prison sits, ending markups on a captive market. It would force competitive bidding for commissary contracts, ban the revenue-sharing arrangements vendors commonly pay prisons for the right to sell, require monthly price reviews, and order an annual government audit of every facility's pricing.
analysis.who_benefits: People incarcerated in federal prisons and their families, who currently pay marked-up prices for soap, food, shoes, and other basics out of money sent in from home. The captive-pricing rule says fair market value must be measured using ordinary retail prices and must exclude prices charged by prisons and other captive markets.

how_it_helps.text: Requires commissary prices to be no greater than the average retail price for the same goods in the state where the facility is located, with a definition that excludes prices at prisons and other captive markets when computing the benchmark [S2].
Bans contracts with revenue-sharing provisions and requires competitive bidding, removing the financial incentive for vendors to charge more and for institutions to accept the kickback [S2].
Requires monthly price reviews, an annual public report to Congress on every facility's prices and contracts, and an annual audit by the Comptroller General to verify compliance [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Commissary contractors, who lose markups and revenue-sharing payments, and the Bureau of Prisons, which loses commissary-generated funds that help pay for inmate programs and amenities.
analysis.who_pays_short: Prison commissary vendors and the BOP

drawbacks.text: Ending commissary revenue could reduce funds the Bureau of Prisons currently generates from commissary sales, some of which support inmate programs, recreation, and amenities, and Congress would need to replace that money directly [S2].
Monthly price reviews across every federal facility plus annual audits create ongoing administrative costs and enforcement work that the bill does not fund [S2].

Retail prices vary widely by state and retailer, so the Director's method for computing fair market value will determine the bill's real effect, and the definition leaves that judgment to the same agency it regulates [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and targeted: ending markups on a captive population of consumers who pay with money their families send in. The main costs are administrative, plus the loss of commissary revenue that currently funds some inmate programs, which is a budgeting problem Congress would need to solve rather than a reason to keep prices inflated. The bill's weak point is not design but support: it has a single sponsor and no cosponsors.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, where it awaits action with no cosponsors and no scheduled consideration.

narrative.text: Rep. Valerie Foushee introduced the bill in the House on July 23, 2026 [S1].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary, which is the only action the bill has received [S4].
No cosponsors have joined the bill [S3].
The bill text directs the Bureau of Prisons to cap commissary prices at state fair market value, requires competitive bidding, and bars revenue-sharing contracts with commissary vendors [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no outcome has been reached; commissary vendors and the Bureau of Prisons keep the status quo pricing arrangement as long as the bill sits without a hearing or vote.

for.name: Rep. Valerie Foushee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Judiciary Committee

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred and no opposition is on the record; with zero cosponsors, no one besides the sponsor has taken a position yet.

industries.note: These vendors sell food, hygiene items, and personal goods to incarcerated people at marked-up prices under contracts that often include revenue-sharing payments to the institutions. The bill caps their prices at ordinary retail and bans those revenue-sharing deals.

industries.industry: Bureau of Prisons (as a revenue recipient)
industries.note: The agency would lose commissary revenue that currently funds some inmate programs and amenities, but would gain a clear pricing mandate, monthly review duties, and oversight in the form of public reports and audits.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has no cosponsors, no committee hearing, and no floor action two weeks into its life in a Congress that ends in early January 2027. Most solo-sponsored bills referred to committee die there without a vote, and this one would need the Judiciary Committee to schedule it and leadership to bring it to the floor, neither of which has any sign of happening.
